strengths: Well-motivated concept: Incorporating fine-grained 3D geometric and semantic structural guidance (via 4D semantic occupancy) addresses the key limitations of trajectory-only video generation, such as gripper misalignment and object distortion.

Comprehensive data curation pipeline: The paper introduces an automated multi-stage pipeline utilizing foundation models (Monst3R, NKSR, Grounding DINO, SAM 2, Qwen-VL) to extract pseudo 4D semantic occupancy from existing large-scale robotic datasets.

Versatile framework extensions: Demonstrates clear potential extensions to multi-view synchronous video generation (ORV-MV) with cross-view attention and simulation-to-real visual domain transfer (ORV-S2R) using simulator-derived occupancy.

Strong image and video fidelity metrics: Substantial numerical improvements in PSNR, SSIM, FID, and FVD over competitive baselines (such as IRASim, CogVideoX, and HMA) across BridgeV2, DROID, and RT-1.
weaknesses: Unclear test-time conditioning and potentially unfair comparison: For the benchmark evaluations on real datasets (BridgeV2, Droid, RT-1 in Table 2), the paper does not specify how future 4D occupancy sequences are obtained at inference time. If future occupancy is extracted/rendered from the ground-truth video, then comparing ORV directly against baselines (like IRASim and HMA) that predict future frames strictly from the initial frame and action commands is fundamentally unfair. If an occupancy dynamics model is used to forecast future occupancy, its details and accuracy are missing from the text.

Lack of downstream robotic policy evaluation: Despite claiming significant utility for embodied AI and robot learning (e.g., imitation learning and sim-to-real transfer), the paper provides no empirical experiments demonstrating policy learning or execution success rates trained on ORV-synthesized videos.

Superficial sim-to-real evaluation: The sim-to-real adaptation (ORV-S2R) is demonstrated through only qualitative examples (Figure 7 and Figure C) without systematic quantitative evaluation against standard sim-to-real visual translation baselines.

Presentation and formatting errors: There are several notable drafting errors, such as referencing 'Table 7' instead of Table 4 in Section 4.4, an incomplete sentence in Section G ('Although we have achieved promising results in , it remains a challenging task...'), and an empty URL placeholder at the end of the abstract.

strengths: Well-motivated approach: Grounding robot video diffusion models with 4D semantic occupancy addresses a key failure mode of purely action-conditioned generation, specifically spatial misalignment and physically implausible object interactions.

Comprehensive framework: The paper develops a full pipeline ranging from automated pseudo-ground-truth 4D semantic occupancy curation (leveraging Monst3R, NKSR, Grounding DINO, SAM2, and Qwen-VL) to multi-view expansion (ORV-MV) and simulation-to-real transfer (ORV-S2R).

Solid quantitative results: The proposed model consistently outperforms prior video prediction baselines (such as IRASim, HMA, and CogVideoX) across three prominent robot manipulation benchmarks (BridgeV2, Droid, and RT-1) in standard metrics (PSNR, SSIM, FID, FVD).

Detailed ablation studies: The authors provide thorough ablations on the role of individual conditioning components (depth vs. semantics, reconstructed vs. rendered condition maps) and base pretraining strategies.
weaknesses: Unclear inference setup and comparison fairness: In Table 2, it is unclear whether ORV is provided with 4D occupancy / rendered condition maps of the entire future trajectory at test time. If future occupancy maps derived from ground-truth video reconstruction are passed as inputs, comparing against action-conditioned future prediction models (such as IRASim or AVID, which predict future dynamics given only the initial observation and action sequence) constitutes an unfair comparison, shifting the problem from future prediction/world modeling to video-to-video / neural rendering.

Lack of downstream robot learning evaluation: While the paper repeatedly motivates ORV as a foundation for robot policy learning and embodied AI simulators, no experiments evaluate policy training (e.g., behavioral cloning or reinforcement learning) on the synthesized videos or evaluate real-world robot task success.

Heavy curation pipeline and computational burden: The 4D annotation pipeline relies on chaining multiple foundation models (Monst3R, NKSR, Qwen-VL, Grounding DINO, SAM2) and consumes substantial storage (8TB for BridgeV2) and compute. The susceptibility of video generation quality to cumulative errors or failures in this multi-stage reconstruction pipeline is not systematically analyzed.

Presentation and writing flaws: Several unresolved references and drafting errors exist in the manuscript (e.g., referencing 'Table 7' instead of 'Table 4' in Section 4.4, and an empty citation/section reference 'Although we have achieved promising results in , it remains...' in Section G on page 26).

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Addressing the coarse alignment and lack of fine-grained spatial control in existing action-conditioned robot video generation models by incorporating 4D semantic occupancy as an intermediate representation is technically sound and timely.

Comprehensive data curation pipeline: Due to the lack of ground-truth 4D semantic occupancy in robot manipulation datasets, the paper designs an effective automated curation pipeline leveraging modern foundation models (Monst3R, NKSR, Grounding DINO, and SAM2) to construct voxelized semantic representations.

Versatile extensions: The framework extends cleanly to multi-view consistent video synthesis (ORV-MV) via view-attention layers and sim-to-real transfer (ORV-S2R) by converting simulator geometries into occupancy representations.

Solid empirical performance on video benchmarks: Quantitative evaluations across BridgeV2, DROID, and RT-1 show consistent and substantial improvements in PSNR, SSIM, FID, and FVD over competitive baselines such as IRASim, HMA, and AVID.
weaknesses: Unclear test-time conditioning assumption / World model rollout: For open-loop future video forecasting from an initial frame and action sequence, where does the future 4D semantic occupancy sequence come from at inference time? If ground-truth or pre-extracted future occupancy sequences are required to render the condition maps, the setting acts more as video neural rendering / re-synthesis rather than an unconstrained predictive world model.

Lack of downstream robotic policy evaluation: Although the paper heavily motivates the framework for robotic imitation learning and sim-to-real transfer, no robot policies (e.g., ACT, Diffusion Policy) are trained or evaluated on the synthesized data to confirm whether the improved visual and geometric realism actually translates to policy performance gains.

Primarily qualitative evaluation for ORV-MV and ORV-S2R: Both the multi-view generation and sim-to-real transfer components are evaluated only through qualitative figures; quantitative multi-view consistency metrics (e.g., multi-view reprojection error) and sim-to-real benchmark metrics are not reported.

Minor presentation errors: In Section 4.4, the text references 'Table 7' when referring to pretraining ablations, but the corresponding table is Table 4. Additionally, Section G contains an incomplete citation/reference placeholder ('results in ,').
